grade.first_issue: The first score-determining defect is the false inference that, when a witness set P_i with i>N meets P(m) and H∩P_i={p}, one must have p∈P(m). The common prime in P_i∩P(m) need not belong to H. This invalidates the central finiteness argument, so Rule E caps the score at 3.
grade.summary: The proof correctly develops finite-stage hitting sets and shows that each S_n is periodic, but it does not establish that the descending sequence S_n stabilizes. The claimed bound on all minimal hitting sets rests on a demonstrably false implication. Repairing this requires a new structural argument controlling the possible primes, not a local correction.
strengths: Correctly relates membership in S_n to hitting sets of the prime-support family.
Correctly observes that each finite-stage set S_n is a finite union of sets of multiples and hence periodic.
The finite-stage enumeration argument is essentially correct after a routine repair, and eventual stabilization of S_n would indeed yield the required translation law.

errors.description: The decisive inference is actually false even for a valid greedy sequence. Take a_1=105; then the next terms are 108,110,112. Here m_n=6 for every n≥3. For n=4, H={3,5,7} is a minimal hitting set, and for p=7 the witness is P_4={2,7}, with 4>N=3 and H∩P_4={7}; nevertheless 7∉P(6)={2,3}. Thus H⊆H_N∪P(m), and hence finiteness and stabilization of the S_n, do not follow.

The assertion that S_n⊆S_{n-1} implies earlier terms in S_{n-1} also lie in S_n reverses the implication of set inclusion. The desired conclusion is readily repaired using the pairwise gcd property supplied when each later term is chosen.
A nondecreasing sequence of positive integers need not stabilize. Here stabilization of m_n can be justified because a_1∈S_n gives m_n≤a_1, but that necessary boundedness argument is omitted.
